title: k8s-gpu-compat-validation-notes
content:
Purpose:
This is a working draft of our private-deployments playbook section focused on Kubernetes + GPU driver / CUDA / NCCL compatibility matrices and validation notes. Intended audience: infra engineers, SREs doing cluster upgrades, and seeding Terraform modules for nodepool creation.

Scope:
- Capture a compact compatibility matrix (K8s, Linux kernel, NVIDIA driver, CUDA, NCCL).
- Capture validation checks to run post-provision and post-upgrade.
- Note Terraform module patterns and gotchas for GPU nodepools.
- Provide an upgrade and rollback outline for GPU-enabled clusters.

Quick summary (opinionated defaults):
- Base OS: Ubuntu 22.04 LTS (kernel 5.15.x) for stable driver support.
- Container runtime: containerd (1.7+) with nvidia-container-toolkit.
- Preferred driver installer: NVIDIA Driver Operator (k8s operator) for cloud-like workflows; image-baked drivers for fully offline/on-prem.
- CUDA compatibility: prefer CUDA runtimes bundled in images (e.g., cuda:12.1-runtime) and ensure driver >= minimum required by image.

Compatibility matrix (human-readable):
Columns: Kubernetes 1.26 / 1.27 / 1.28 ; Kernel baseline; NVIDIA driver recommended (tested); CUDA runtime range; NCCL tested
- K8s 1.26 | kernel 5.15.x | driver 525.105+ | CUDA 11.8 - 12.0 | NCCL 2.14
- K8s 1.27 | kernel 5.15.x / 6.1.x | driver 535.86+ | CUDA 11.8 - 12.1 | NCCL 2.14 - 2.16
- K8s 1.28 | kernel 6.1.x | driver 540.48+ | CUDA 12.0 - 12.2 | NCCL 2.16 - 2.18
Notes on matrix: these are compiled from internal runs across p4/p40/a100 type nodes and public NVIDIA compatibility docs. The driver column indicates the minimum recommended; prefer +2 minor versions for production for stability. If using GPUs with Ampere+/Hopper+ architecture, target driver 535+ as baseline.

Validation checklist (post-provision):
1) Node and driver basic sanity:
   - ssh to node -> run `uname -r` and `nvidia-smi` (expect driver version matches plan)
   - check dmesg for GPU driver errors (look for UVM, memory alloc failures)
2) Container runtime integration:
   - run `ctr run --rm --runtime "io.containerd.runc.v2" docker.io/nvidia/cuda:12.1-runtime nvidia-check nvidia-smi` (should show GPUs)
   - kubectl apply a tiny pod using runtimeClass (if used) and ensure `kubectl describe pod` shows GPU resource allocated
3) CUDA functional test:
   - run a CUDA sample (vectorAdd) in privileged container or using NVIDIA CUDA container and check for expected output and non-zero throughput
4) NCCL smoke test (multinode if available):
   - run NCCL allreduce microbench across 2+ GPU nodes (use ibverbs/rdma disabled or enabled depending on network)
   - validate that peak bandwidth and no NACKs/errors are seen in logs
5) Workload-level regression test:
   - deploy a small inference replica (FP16) and assert tail latency and throughput within expected baseline
6) Observability checks:
   - metrics: node exporter + DCGM exporter showing GPU metrics, NVML counters
   - traces/logs: no OOM errors, kernel GPU panics
7) Security checks:
   - secure boot: confirm whether driver is signed, if secure boot on must use DKMS-signed builds or kernel module signing workflow

Terraform module notes (practical patterns):
- Module inputs (recommended): node_pool_gpu_count, gpu_sku (e.g., a100-40g), gpu_taints, gpu_labels, image_id_or_bake, driver_install_method (operator|baked|daemonset), preemptible (bool), max_pods.
- Avoid remote-exec driver install at scale during create -- it races and is brittle. Prefer image baked with drivers or use NVIDIA operator which reconciles reliably.
- Provide lifecycle.replace_triggered_by for kernel updates (example: `lifecycle { replace_triggered_by = [var.kernel_version] }`) so node recreates when image/kernel changes are intentional.
- Expose a `driver_version` variable that ties expectations into Terraform plan outputs (so PR reviewers see driver delta).
- Create an output `node_gpu_validation_script` that prints a small script/fingerprint the SRE can run on node for immediate smoke tests (nvidia-smi, cuda sample).
- Document integration with image build pipeline (packer/ami) for on-prem images; maintain a small artifact registry of tested image+driver+kernel tuples.

Driver and operator tradeoffs:
- Operator (NVIDIA driver operator / Device Plugin operator):
   Pros: declarative, supports air-gapped via registry images, handles kernel module injection in place, easier for rolling upgrades.
   Cons: additional moving part, needs RBAC and cluster privileges.
- Baked image:
   Pros: simplest runtime, predictable boot time, fewer dynamic installs.
   Cons: need new image build for driver updates; large image surface.

Upgrade plan (GPU-aware Kubernetes upgrade):
Pre-upgrade:
- Run full validation checklist and store results (snapshots of `nvidia-smi`, CUDA test outputs, metrics) in a known S3/MinIO bucket.
- Ensure workloads are marked (labels) and have PodDisruptionBudgets defined for critical inference services.
- Notify application owners and open brief maintenance ticket.

Stepwise upgrade (recommended):
1) Control plane upgrade first (standard kubeadm/kops/GKE-flow).
2) Validate control plane health and kubelet versions across nodes.
3) Upgrade non-GPU nodepools first (if exist).
4) For GPU nodepools: process one node at a time for driver-sensitive workloads:
   a) cordon node `kubectl cordon <node>`
   b) drain node `kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --force-if-needed`
   c) if using baked image: recreate node with new image/kernel matching target driver; verify boot + `nvidia-smi`
   d) if using operator: upgrade operator + driver image, wait for DaemonSet or operator to reconcile drivers, then `kubectl rollout status` for operator pods
   e) run node-level validation (CUDA sample, container runtime test, NCCL microbench if multinode possible)
   f) uncordon node
5) Proceed to next GPU node.
6) After all GPU nodes upgraded, run cluster-level E2E tests (inference smoke, throughput, mem leak checks).

Driver upgrade ordering note:
- We recommend upgrading Kubernetes first (control plane), then driver/operator, then CUDA/container images if needed. Historically, upgrading driver before control plane can leave nodes kubelet-incompatible.

Rollback strategy:
- Node-level rollback: if validation fails on a node, reprovision from snapshot of previous image or redeploy previous driver via operator. Keep images for the previous driver available in local registry.
- Cluster-level rollback: use Velero to restore critical namespace state if persistent workloads fail. For stateful services, have DB backups.
- Terraform: use `terraform apply` to revert to previous nodepool instance counts/images; for destructive changes, prefer re-create instead of in-place driver downgrade.

Common failure modes and remediation (notes):
- Symptom: nvidia-smi reports NVML init failed after kernel update -> likely mismatched kernel/driver; remediation: reboot into kernel matching driver or reinstall driver built for current kernel.
- Symptom: pods schedule but show GPU allocation missing -> check device plugin logs (nvidia-device-plugin) and node allocatable resources; check CRI plugin logs for nvidia-container-toolkit.
- Symptom: NCCL hangs with `NCCL WARN` messages -> check network MTU, ibverbs stack, and if using VPC, ensure RDMA or correct network fabric is configured; try NCCL_TCP if RDMA not available.
- Symptom: long node boot times -> driver postinstall scripts or DKMS compile choking; use precompiled kernel module in images for faster boots.

Validation automation suggestions (future work items):
- Add a Terraform `null_resource` with local-exec that triggers a remote smoke-runner in CI to validate newly created nodes automatically (only in non-prod).
- CI nightly matrix that spins up minimal 1-node GPU cluster per matrix row (k8s version x driver version) and runs smoke tests, archives logs.
- Integrate DCGM exporter metrics into our alerting for driver anomalies (NVML errors, ECC counts).

Open questions / TODOs:
- Finalize our supported K8s versions policy for private deployments (EOL cadence + driver support window).
- Decide whether to standardize on Operator vs baked image for customer on-prem bundles (tradeoffs around air-gap).
- Add exact test thresholds for NCCL bandwidth and inference tail latency baselines (collect more production samples).

Appendix: quick commands
- Node smoke script snippet (to paste into `node_gpu_validation_script` output):
  #!/bin/bash
  set -e
  echo "kernel: $(uname -r)"
  echo "nvidia-smi:"
  nvidia-smi || (echo 'nvidia-smi failed' && exit 2)
  docker run --rm --gpus all --entrypoint nvidia-smi nvidia/cuda:12.1-runtime || echo 'container runtime test failed'
  echo 'run simple CUDA vectorAdd test (left as exercise)';

- Kube drain that preserves daemonsets:
  kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --timeout=10m

Contact: Aisha Patel (infra) — reach out on #infra-private-deployments for syncs.

End of draft.
